body: Coursera is a global online learning platform where learners take short, self-paced Courses to build practical skills and apply what they learn. Duke's Learning Experience Design team partners with faculty to shape those experiences for an asynchronous, global audience.

This guide walks through the different levels of Coursera design, from the larger learning journey to individual learning assets. It is intended to be used alongside the Design Document you'll complete with your Learning Experience Designer.

mapping.title: How your course maps to Coursera
mapping.intro: These are rough comparisons rather than one-to-one equivalents. Designing for Coursera usually means narrowing and reshaping existing material rather than simply dividing a semester Course into smaller pieces.

rows.fromDetail: Often several weeks of your syllabus

rows.fromLabel: A lecture, reading, activity, or assessment

note.title: What counts as learner time
note.body: Learner time includes videos, readings, quizzes, practice activities, projects, and any other work required to complete the Course. Estimate the time the learner spends, not the amount of material you provide.

structure.title: How a Coursera learning experience fits together

specialization.question: What larger goal are learners working toward?

courses.question: What meaningful skills should learners develop?

modules.question: What smaller learning steps will help them get there?

assets.title: Learning Assets
assets.question: What experience will best support each step?

reuse.title: Can you use what you already have?
reuse.lead: In most cases, yes! Your Learning Experience Designer will work with you to ensure that your materials are cleared for public, commercial use. Here's what we will look at together.

items.label: Start with skills
items.body: Coursera learners are often working professionals who are building a specific skill. We'll start with what learners should be able to do by the end, then work backward to the materials, framing, and assessments that will help them get there.

items.label: Keep videos focused
items.body: Learners tend to engage best with videos under about 10 minutes. If you have longer recordings, we can help identify natural breaks and shape them into shorter, more focused segments.

items.label: Balance learning formats
items.body: Readings can be valuable, but a course made up mostly of readings may not provide enough variety or practice. We'll look together at where a video, audio conversation, visual, or hands-on activity might communicate an idea more effectively.

items.label: Build in accessibility
items.body: Captions, transcripts, alt text, and readable color contrast help make a course accessible to more learners. These elements are much easier to address during planning than after materials have been produced.

items.label: Check content permissions
items.body: Images, figures, video clips, datasets, and other materials you didn't create may require permission or an appropriate license. We'll review materials together to make sure they can be used with a public, global audience, including for commercial purposes.

items.label: Plan for tool access
items.body: If your course depends on particular software or external tools, we'll look for a free or widely available option whenever possible. Paid or license-restricted tools may be out of reach for learners outside Duke or unavailable in some countries, so where a tool is essential, we'll plan together for how learners can access it.

handoff.title: Ready to plan yours?
handoff.body: The template is the blank version of everything here to get started.

specialization.label: SPECIALIZATION
specialization.title: Designing a Coursera Specialization
lede: A Coursera Specialization brings several Courses together into a purposeful learning journey, with each Course helping learners build toward a larger skill or goal.

Unlike students enrolled in a traditional Duke course, Coursera learners choose whether and when to participate. They may be working, balancing other responsibilities, or taking only one Course within a larger pathway. They are likely to ask:

lede.question: Is this for me? What will I be able to do? And is it worth the time?

lede: Begin by identifying the learners you hope to reach, the goals they are working toward, and the skills they should develop by the end of the Specialization.

sections.title: Define the goal
body: A strong Specialization begins with a clear learner need and a meaningful end goal. Before planning individual Courses, identify who the experience is for, what they are trying to accomplish, and what they should be able to do by the end.
Coursera learners often choose learning based on its relevance, usefulness, and fit with their available time. Make it easy for them to recognize the value of the experience.
Keep in mind:

bullets.rest: Help learners quickly understand who the Specialization is for, what it will help them accomplish, and why that matters.
Focus on skills and knowledge learners can use in a professional, academic, or other real-world context.
Prioritize what is essential and design toward a focused, achievable outcome.

anchor.label: A helpful question
anchor.body: What should learners be able to do by the end of this Specialization?

children.title: A Specialization goal
body: Learners will be able to use business data to identify meaningful findings, communicate insights, and make evidence-informed recommendations.

sections.title: Shape the journey
body: How should the Courses work together to help learners reach that goal?

Courses may introduce, develop, integrate, or apply different skills. Some Specializations work best as a clear progression in which each Course builds on the one before it. Others may include Courses that are more modular and useful on their own.
There is no single required structure. What matters is that each Course has a distinct purpose and that the relationship among the Courses is intentional and easy for learners to understand.

left.label: Rather than asking
left.body: How should I divide my content into three Courses?

right.label: You might ask
right.body: What should each Course contribute to the larger learner journey?

children.title: Data Analytics for Business Decisions

items.type: Foundations of Data Analytics for Business
items.what: Learners frame a business question and identify and prepare the data needed to investigate it.
Learners analyze data and create visualizations that reveal meaningful patterns and trends.
Learners use their findings to develop and communicate an evidence-informed recommendation.

children.footnote: Together, the Courses create a clear progression: **Frame and prepare → Analyze and visualize → Recommend and communicate**. Each Course has a recognizable purpose of its own while contributing to the larger Specialization goal.

sections.title: Complete your Specialization plan
sections.note: Use this page to work through the decisions, then record them in the Design Document.

rows.label: Specialization title
rows.hint: Choose a clear, compelling title that helps the right learners discover your Specialization.

advice.best: Write for the learner deciding whether to click. A strong title makes the **topic and value of the Specialization immediately clear**. Favor specific, familiar language over academic or internally meaningful terminology.

rows.label: About this Specialization
rows.hint: Create a 2-3 sentence summary of the content, learning outcomes, and any industry partners. Highlight the main value or application learners will get from the Specialization.

advice.best: Lead with what learners will **gain or be able to do**, rather than with a list of topics. Help learners quickly understand who the Specialization is for, what they will experience, and why it is worth their time.

paras: Learn to use data to answer business questions and make evidence-informed recommendations. Across three courses, you'll practice working with real-world datasets, identify patterns and trends, create clear visualizations, and communicate insights to support better decisions.

rows.label: Projects overview
rows.hint: In 1-2 sentences, describe the nature of the included projects and how learners will apply the skills to solve an authentic problem.

advice.best: Describe what learners will **make, analyze, evaluate, or solve**. Projects should reflect realistic situations learners may encounter beyond the course — not simply serve as longer versions of quizzes.

paras: Learners will analyze business data to investigate a practical question, identify meaningful trends, create visualizations, and recommend an action. Projects are designed around common workplace tasks such as evaluating customer behavior, monitoring performance, or identifying opportunities for improvement.

advice.best: Describe learners in terms they are likely to recognize: their **role, goals, or reasons for learning**. Be specific enough to help the right learners identify themselves, while avoiding requirements that unnecessarily exclude interested learners.

paras: Early-career professionals, managers, analysts, and other business professionals who want to use data more confidently in their day-to-day work.

advice.best: Include only the knowledge or experience learners **actually need to succeed**. Distinguish essential preparation from helpful context so that ideal qualifications do not become unnecessary barriers to enrollment.

paras: No prior experience in data analytics or programming is required. Familiarity with basic workplace math and an interest in using data to support decisions will be helpful.

rows.label: What will you learn
rows.hint: Write 1-3 actionable, measurable learning objectives that describe what learners will be able to do by the end of the Specialization.

advice.best: Describe **observable capabilities**, not topics learners will encounter or ideas they will “understand.” Begin with an action verb such as **evaluate, apply, analyze, design,** or **recommend**, and make sure the objectives represent the **full Specialization**, not just one course.

example.lead: By the end of the Specialization, learners will be able to:
bullets: **Analyze** business datasets to identify patterns, trends, and relevant findings.
**Create** clear data visualizations that communicate insights to a defined audience.
**Recommend** evidence-informed actions in response to a business question.

advice.best: Name **specific, recognizable skills learners can demonstrate**, rather than broad subject areas. Choose terms learners might use to describe their capabilities on a résumé, on LinkedIn, or in a conversation with an employer.

swap.consider: Data Cleaning · Exploratory Data Analysis · Data Visualization · Spreadsheet Analysis · Business Intelligence · Data Storytelling · Evidence-Based Decision-Making

advice.best: Estimate the learner's **total experience**, not just the length of the instructional content. Include time for watching, reading, practicing, completing projects, and taking assessments. Account for the reality that Coursera learners often study in shorter sessions around other responsibilities.

paras: Three courses of approximately eight hours each, including instruction, practice, assessments, and projects.

advice.best: Choose the level based on the **knowledge, skills, and independence required of the learner**, not on the sophistication of the subject itself. A complex topic can still be appropriate for beginners when concepts are introduced from the ground up.

paras: **Beginner** — No previous experience with data analytics or programming is required. Learners will be guided through foundational concepts and tools before completing independent analyses.

rows.label: Tools, technology, or platforms
rows.ph: [ any required external tools or access ]

advice.best: Identify anything learners need to **access or use to complete the learning experience**, including external tools, software, accounts, or platforms. Make requirements visible early, and flag any paid licenses or institutional access requirements.

paras: Learners will need access to a web browser and spreadsheet software. All required datasets and practice materials will be provided. No specialized or institution-restricted software is required.

Course title.best: Give each course a **distinct purpose within the larger learner journey**. Learners should be able to see how their capabilities will develop from one course to the next.

bullets: **Foundations of Data Analytics for Business**
**Analyzing and Visualizing Business Data**
**Communicating Data-Driven Recommendations**
example.note: The progression tells a clear story: **learn the foundations → analyze the data → communicate and act on the findings**.

Main outcomes.best: Give each course an outcome that is **meaningful on its own while contributing to the larger Specialization outcome**. Organize courses around meaningful stages of the work learners will do, rather than dividing them simply by topic or amount of content.

rows: Foundations of Data Analytics for Business
Frame a business question and identify the data needed to investigate it.
Analyze a business dataset and create visualizations that reveal relevant patterns and trends.
Develop and communicate an evidence-informed recommendation for a business audience.

Est. time.best: Aim for a **reasonable and relatively balanced learner experience across courses**, while allowing the work itself to determine the exact length. Include all learning activities (i.e., video, readings, activities, and assessments) in this estimate.

rows.label: Specialization project or culminating experience (optional)
rows.ph: [ description and source link, if applicable ]

advice.best: Use a culminating experience to help learners **integrate skills from across the Specialization**, rather than simply repeat an assignment from the final course. Give learners a realistic problem, decision, product, or scenario that requires them to draw on multiple capabilities.

paras: Learners will investigate a business question using a provided dataset, clean and analyze the data, create visualizations to communicate key findings, and develop an evidence-informed recommendation for a business audience.

course.label: COURSE
course.title: Planning a Course
lede: A Coursera Course offers a focused learning experience that helps learners develop specific skills and achieve a meaningful outcome.
A helpful place to begin is by defining the Course's distinct contribution.

lede.question: What should learners be able to do by the end of this Course?

lede: You can then translate that purpose into a small set of Course-level objectives. These objectives will guide the design of the Modules, where you'll break the larger capabilities into manageable stages and begin aligning them with opportunities for practice and assessment.

sections.title: Write Course objectives
body: Once the Course has a clear purpose, translate that purpose into 2–4 course-level learning objectives. A strong Course objective describes something learners can demonstrate by the end of the Course. It should be broad enough for several Modules to contribute to its development, while still being achievable within the Course itself.

rungs.example: Evaluate the quality of a dataset

rungs.gloss: What learners can do in a meaningful context
rungs.example: Evaluate whether available data is appropriate for investigating a business question

sections.prompt: By the end of this Course, learners will be able to…
sections.goodLabel: Consider using observable action verbs such as
sections.weakLabel: These verbs may need more specificity
sections.weakNote: They may describe your instructional intention, but they do not clearly indicate what learners will be able to demonstrate.

children.title: Objectives for a sample Course
body: For Foundations of Data Analytics for Business, learners will be able to:

bullets.rest: a business need into a focused question that can be investigated with data.
the data needed to investigate a business question.
a dataset for relevance, completeness, and basic quality concerns.
data for an introductory business analysis.

items.heading: Is it observable?
items.body: Could learners demonstrate the objective through something they do, create, analyze, evaluate, or decide?

items.heading: Is it achievable within this Course?
items.body: Can learners reasonably reach the objective through the instruction, practice, feedback, and assessment included in the Course?

items.heading: Is it meaningful to learners?
items.body: Does the capability have recognizable value beyond completing the Course? Can learners see how they might use it in a professional, academic, or other real-world context?

items.heading: Is it appropriate for a self-paced online experience?
items.body: Can learners build and demonstrate the capability without depending on live discussion, immediate instructor support, or synchronous participation?

items.heading: If this Course is part of a larger learning pathway, does it fit?
items.body: Do the objectives support the broader goals of the Specialization, certificate, or program while still giving the Course a clear purpose of its own?

sections.title: Focus the Course scope
body: Now that you've checked your objectives, use them to guide decisions about the Course's scope.
For each topic, resource, or activity, ask:

bullets: What knowledge or skills will learners gain from this?
Will they need it to achieve the Course objectives?
Will it help them practice or demonstrate what they should be able to do?

body: These questions can help you decide what to include, what to leave out, and how to organize the learning around the Course's purpose. A strong Course is not simply a collection of related topics; each element should help learners develop the knowledge and skills they need to achieve the intended outcomes.

left.label: Rather than asking
left.body: Which topics should this Course cover?

right.label: You might ask
right.body: What knowledge and skills do learners need to achieve the Course objectives?

children.title: Using a Course objective to guide scope

anchor.label: Course objective
anchor.body: Learners will be able to prepare data for an introductory business analysis.

left.label: Include
bullets: Identifying relevant data fields
Checking for missing or inconsistent values
Restructuring a simple dataset
Documenting data-preparation decisions

right.label: Consider leaving out
bullets: Advanced statistical modeling
Complex programming techniques
Topics that do not support the introductory analysis

sections.title: Design for flexibility
body: Coursera Courses often work well when they are modular and self-contained. When possible, provide enough context for learners to understand the Course's purpose, why the learning matters, and what prior knowledge or skills they need to succeed without requiring them to have completed a specific earlier Course.

Some subjects are best learned through a sequence. When learners genuinely need knowledge or skills from an earlier Course, make that dependency clear. The goal is not to eliminate prerequisites, but to make Courses as portable and understandable on their own as the learning allows.

left.label: More dependent on a specific sequence
left.body: As you learned in Course 1, you will now build on the framework introduced in Module 3…

right.label: More modular
right.body: This course assumes familiarity with basic spreadsheet formulas and functions.

sections.title: Complete your Course plan
sections.note: Use this page to work through the decisions, then record them in the Design Document. This section repeats for each course.

rows.label: Course title
rows.hint: Choose a clear, compelling title that helps the right learners discover your Course.

advice.best: Write for the learner deciding whether this Course is relevant to them. A strong title makes the **topic and learner value immediately clear** while giving the Course a distinct purpose. Favor specific, familiar language over academic numbering or internal terminology.

swap.consider: Foundations of Data Analytics for Business

rows.label: Course description
rows.hint: Draft a learner-friendly 2-3 sentence summary of the content and learning outcomes. Highlight the main value or application learners will get from the Course.

advice.best: Describe the Course from the learner's perspective. Lead with what learners will **gain or be able to do**, rather than with a list of topics. Provide enough context for the Course to make sense on its own, even when it is part of a larger learning pathway.

paras: Learn how to turn a business need into a question that data can help answer. You'll practice identifying useful data, evaluating its relevance and quality, and preparing data for an introductory analysis using realistic business examples.

advice.best: Estimate the learner's **total experience**, including videos, readings, practice, activities, and assessments — not just instructional content. Keep the scope realistic for a self-paced Coursera Course that learners may complete in shorter sessions around other responsibilities.

paras: **Approximately 7 hours**, including instruction, guided practice, assessments, and applied activities.

advice.best: Choose the level based on the **knowledge, skills, and independence learners need to succeed**, not on how sophisticated the subject sounds. A complex topic can still be appropriate for beginners when foundational concepts and sufficient support are built into the Course.

paras: **Beginner** — No prior data analytics or programming experience is required. Learners will be introduced to foundational concepts and guided through their first data-focused business tasks.

advice.best: Choose the category that most directly reflects the **Course's primary subject and learner value**. Use the most specific appropriate Coursera domain rather than trying to represent every discipline the Course touches.
Use a secondary domain when another area meaningfully represents the Course. It should describe a substantial part of the learning experience, not simply broaden discoverability.

Choose **specific skills learners will actively practice or demonstrate in this Course**. Avoid broad subject labels, and select tags that align closely with the Course objectives, activities, and assessments.

swap.consider: Business Problem Framing · Data Requirements Analysis · Data Quality Assessment · Spreadsheet Analysis · Exploratory Data Analysis

rows.label: Recommended background
rows.ph: [ what learners should know before starting ]

advice.best: Include only the knowledge or experience learners **actually need before beginning the Course**. Distinguish true prerequisites from experience that may simply be helpful, and avoid creating unnecessary barriers for otherwise appropriate learners.

paras: No prior experience with data analytics or programming is required. Basic familiarity with spreadsheets and workplace math will be helpful.

rows.label: What learners will learn
rows.ph:
1. [ objective ]
2. [ objective ]
3. [ objective, optional ]
4. [ objective, optional ]
rows.hint: Write 2-4 actionable, measurable learning objectives that describe what learners will be able to do by the end of the Course.

best: Write **2–4 observable, measurable Course objectives** that describe meaningful capabilities learners should be able to demonstrate by the end of the Course. Objectives should be achievable within the Course and valuable to learners beyond simply completing it.

Begin with action verbs such as **analyze, apply, create, evaluate, identify, interpret, recommend,** or **communicate**. Verbs such as *understand, learn,* or *become familiar with* may describe your instructional intention, but they do not clearly indicate what learners will be able to demonstrate.

example.lead: By the end of the Course, learners will be able to:
bullets: **Translate** a business need into a focused question that can be investigated with data.
**Identify** the data needed to investigate a business question.
**Evaluate** a dataset for relevance, completeness, and basic quality concerns.
**Prepare** data for an introductory business analysis.
example.note: These objectives give the Course a clear purpose and provide a foundation for planning Module-level objectives, activities, and assessments.

rows.label: Instructor information and bio source link
rows.ph: [ bio text, or link to build-ready bio and headshot ]

best: Provide concise, learner-facing information that establishes the instructor's **relevant expertise and connection to the Course topic**. Prioritize experience that helps learners understand why this instructor is well positioned to guide the learning experience.
If an approved faculty bio and headshot already exist, provide a build-ready source link rather than recreating the material.

paras: Jordan Lee is a faculty member specializing in business analytics and evidence-informed decision-making. Their teaching and research focus on helping organizations use data to frame questions, evaluate performance, and make more informed decisions.
*Source: [link to approved faculty bio and headshot]*

module.label: MODULE
module.title: Designing a Coursera Module
lede: A Module is a focused part of a Course that helps learners move from encountering a new idea to using it themselves. It typically includes some combination of explanation, examples, practice, feedback, and assessment.

In a face-to-face course, you can adjust your explanation when learners look confused, answer questions as they arise, and provide clarification in the moment. In an asynchronous Coursera Course, learners move through the experience on their own and may not have an instructor or classmate available when a question arises.
A well-designed Module builds the necessary structure and support into the learning experience. Learners should be able to understand:

bullets: What are they trying to do?
Why does it matter?
What do they need to know first?
Where can they try it?
How will they know whether they are on the right track?
What can they do if they get stuck?

lede: This does not mean eliminating challenge or anticipating every possible question. It means giving learners a clear path forward.

sections.title: A helpful way to plan
sections.after: The sequence may not always be linear. Learners may move back and forth between preparation and practice, but each element should help them work toward the Module objectives.

sections.title: Start with the learner's next step
body: Course objectives describe the larger skills learners should develop by the end of the Course. Module objectives break those skills into smaller, achievable steps.

left.label: Rather than asking
left.body: What topics should I cover in this Module?

right.label: You might ask
right.body: What should learners be able to do next as they work toward the Course objective?

sections.note: A Module might introduce a concept, guide learners through a process, help them analyze an example, or give them an opportunity to apply a skill in a realistic situation.

sections.title: Example: from Course objective to Module objectives

anchor.label: Course objective
anchor.body: Analyze business datasets to identify patterns, trends, and relevant findings.

body: **Module objectives** — by the end of this Module, learners will be able to:

bullets: Identify variables relevant to a business question.
Calculate appropriate summary measures for a dataset.
Interpret those measures in the context of the business question.

sections.after: These objectives are narrower than the Course objective, but each one helps learners move toward it.

sections.title: Keep Module objectives actionable
body: Describe something learners can demonstrate, rather than simply a topic they will encounter or something they will “understand.”
sections.after: The Module planning template calls for approximately **1–3** actionable, measurable learning objectives per Module.

sections.title: 1. Define what learners will do
body: Once you have identified the Module objectives, decide what learners will do to show that they are making progress toward them.

anchor.label: Ask
anchor.body: What would convince you that learners achieved this objective?

body: The verb in the objective can help you choose an appropriate form of assessment.

rows: Classifying examples or responding to scenario-based questions
Completing a problem, exercise, lab, or task
Examining a dataset, case, artifact, or scenario
Applying criteria, weighing evidence, and making a decision
Producing an artifact, plan, solution, or response

body: The assessment should ask learners to demonstrate the same kind of thinking or performance described in the objective.

anchor.label: A useful question
anchor.body: If I could see only one thing learners did in this Module, what would show me they achieved the objective?

body: The answer does not need to be an elaborate project. It does need to provide evidence of the intended learning.

anchor.label: Example — objective
anchor.body: Interpret summary measures in the context of a business question.

body: **Possible assessment** — learners review summary statistics from a customer dataset and identify which conclusions are supported by the data. Feedback explains why each response is or is not appropriate.

sections.title: 2. Prepare learners to get started
body: After deciding what learners will do, identify what they need before they can complete the task successfully.

anchor.label: Ask
anchor.body: What does a learner need to know, see, or use before attempting this activity?

body: Preparation might include a brief explanation of a new concept, a demonstration or worked example, a reading or reference guide, an expert conversation, a model or annotated example, a job aid, template, or checklist, background information about a case, or instructions for accessing a tool, dataset, or platform.

anchor.label: Rather than starting with
anchor.body: What videos do I need to record?

anchor.label: Start with
anchor.body: What does the learner need in order to succeed?

body: Then choose the format that best supports that need.

bullets.rest: may help with explaining a difficult idea, demonstrating a process, walking through an example, introducing a case, or bringing instructor presence into the Course.
may work better for detailed reference information, material learners may want to revisit, definitions, procedures, or examples, or content learners need to scan quickly.
may be the best way to introduce a process learners will need to perform.
may be useful for an expert perspective, conversation, or narrative explanation.

sections.after: You do not need to select every format here. The Learning Assets page provides more detailed guidance on Coursera formats and when each one may be useful.

sections.title: Make the invisible visible
body: In a classroom, learners can often infer what matters from your emphasis, gestures, examples, and responses to questions. In an asynchronous Course, those cues need to be made more explicit.
For each important activity, consider telling learners:

bullets: why the topic or task matters;
what they should pay attention to;
what they are expected to do;
how much time the activity may take;
what a successful response includes;
whether the activity is for practice or a grade;
what to do if they are unsure; and
how the activity connects to the larger Course objective.

sections.after: These details may feel obvious to an instructor, but they help learners navigate the experience independently.

sections.title: 3. Give learners a chance to practice
body: Once you know what learners will do to demonstrate the objective, ask:

anchor.label: Ask
anchor.body: What will learners need to try before they are ready to succeed on the assessment?

body: Learners should practice the same kind of thinking or performance they will later be asked to demonstrate. Practice should not simply repeat information from a video; it should give learners an opportunity to use what they are learning. Depending on the objective, learners might:

bullets: work through a realistic case or scenario;
analyze a dataset;
complete a guided lab or programming exercise;
make a decision using defined criteria;
use a template, framework, or checklist;
respond to an application or reflection prompt;
practice a professional interaction; or
answer questions and receive feedback before a graded attempt.

body: For hands-on work, provide enough structure for learners to get started while preserving an appropriate level of challenge. Useful supports might include a sample file, a model, a checklist, a hint, or a partially completed example.

sections.title: Build in both practice and demonstration
body: Not every assessment needs to be graded.

**Practice assessments** give learners low-stakes opportunities to ask whether they can do this yet. They can help learners check their understanding, identify misconceptions, and receive feedback before a graded attempt.

**Graded assessments** provide evidence that learners have achieved the Module objectives. Each Coursera Module requires at least one graded assessment, and Course-level objectives should be represented in the Course's graded assessments.

For many Modules, an auto-graded quiz with meaningful feedback can be an effective option. Other formats — including labs, programming assignments, and assignments that evaluate submitted work — may be more appropriate when learners need to perform or create something.

Practice quizzes should rehearse the thinking required by the graded assessment. Feedback should help learners understand why an answer is correct or incorrect, not simply indicate whether they got it right.
sections.after: Choose the assessment based on the objective, not the other way around.

sections.title: Design for moments when learners get stuck
body: Asynchronous learners may not be able to ask a question at the moment they need help. As you plan each activity, consider what support you can build into the experience. Learners may benefit from:

bullets: clear instructions and success criteria;
setup details and technology requirements;
a defined deliverable;
worked examples;
step-by-step guidance for unfamiliar tasks;
templates, frameworks, or checklists;
hints or optional scaffolding;
feedback for both correct and incorrect responses;
opportunities to retry when appropriate;
links back to relevant content; and
model responses or explanations after practice.

anchor.label: Ask
anchor.body: If a learner gets stuck here, what might help them take the next step?

body: The goal is not to remove productive challenge. It is to provide a clear path forward without requiring an instructor or peer to be available in the moment.
sections.after: For hands-on practice, clear setup details, defined deliverables, and opportunities for low-stakes trial and error can be especially helpful.

sections.title: Example: build a Module backward

anchor.label: Course objective
anchor.body: Analyze business datasets to identify patterns, trends, and relevant findings.

steps.label: Define
steps.caption: **Module objective** — interpret summary measures in the context of a business question.

items.label: Video
items.body: Choosing and interpreting common summary measures

items.label: Reading
items.body: Quick reference: when to use mean, median, range, and percentage

items.label: Worked example
items.body: From customer data to a business insight

items.label: Learner support
items.body: A step-by-step checklist for interpreting summary measures in context

items.label: Guided case activity
items.body: Learners calculate and interpret summary measures for a smaller dataset. Prompts help them connect the results to a business question.

items.label: Practice check
items.body: Learners respond to scenario-based questions and receive feedback explaining common interpretation errors.

items.label: Graded assessment
items.body: Learners review summary statistics from a customer dataset and determine which conclusions are supported by the evidence.

sections.after: Each element has a clear purpose because it connects back to the same Module objective.

sections.title: Think of the Module as a learning pathway
body: A strong Module gives learners a clear path from preparation to successful application. Each stage below pairs what you are designing with what the learner experiences.
sections.after: The exact mix will vary. Some Modules may require more explanation, while others may center on a substantial hands-on activity or project. What matters is that each element helps learners move toward the Module objectives.

sections.title: Before you finalize a Module

bullets.rest: Is it clear what learners are learning to do?
Is the learning step small enough to be manageable?
Does the graded task match the objective?
Have learners had a chance to try the same kind of work?
Do they have the knowledge, examples, and tools they need?
Will they learn why a response is or is not successful?
Will they know what to do, why it matters, and what comes next?
Can they continue if an instructor or peer is not immediately available?

body: As you plan, keep asking: what should learners be able to do, how will they demonstrate it, what practice will help them get there, what do they need to know, see, or use first, and what support will help them continue if they get stuck?

sections.title: Choosing the formats
body: On the Learning Assets page you'll explore the Coursera formats available for delivering each part of the experience — from videos and readings to hands-on practice, interactive tools, Dialogue, practice quizzes, and graded assessments.

sections.title: What you'll fill in
sections.note: Use this page to work through the decisions, then record them in the Design Document. This section repeats for every module.

rows.label: Module title
rows.hint: Draft what learners will learn, do, or produce in this Module.

rows.label: Module description
rows.hint: Draft a learner-friendly 2-3 sentence summary of the Module content and learning outcomes.

rows.label: Module learning objectives
rows.hint: Write 1-3 actionable, measurable learning objectives that describe what learners will be able to do by the end of the Module.

rows.text: For anything created outside this template, please include a link to the final or draft source. This will help your Learning Experience Designer build the content directly from the source. Lessons are optional, so you may leave this column blank or remove it if you're not using lessons.
Aim for a minimum of: 3–6 videos · 1–2 readings · 1–2 activities · 1 auto-graded quiz

rows.label: Additional build notes, dependencies, or accessibility information

rows.title: Course 1 · Module 1 Graded Quiz
rows.text: Before writing your questions, please review the Coursera Graded Quiz Template and Guidelines. The quiz should assess the objectives for this module.

assets.label: LEARNING ASSETS
assets.title: Learning assets
assets.lede: The individual items learners watch, read, and do. Each type has its own pedagogy, accessibility requirements, and copyright considerations.
assets.alsoAvailable: Also available: in-video questions, code blocks, programming assignments, Coursera Labs, AI-graded assignments, and external tools via LTI.

items.title: Video
items.what: Videos introduce and teach a course topic. Video is powerful for human connection, storytelling, and demonstration — the moments where learners benefit from seeing a real person.
pedagogy: Aim for 5–10 minutes, one idea per video.

Chunking is the whole game. Shorter videos hold attention; longer ones often get skipped entirely. Videos under 10 minutes increase lecture completion rates by 16% and raise satisfaction with the course overall.
The strongest-performing courses keep at least two-thirds of their videos under 10 minutes. Break complex topics into a series of short, focused videos with clear, specific titles.
What raises engagement: open with a hook or story, keep the tone conversational, use appropriate humor, add visuals or animation, and keep a relatively brisk speaking pace.
Try not to default to video. Readings, interactives, and labs are often better for reference material and anything that needs frequent updating.
Use AI tools to speed up production, but aim to keep a real person as the on-screen presenter — learners benefit from seeing real people.
accessibility: Accurate captions are required, and a transcript should be available.
Say aloud what's on screen — try not to rely on visuals alone to carry meaning.
Check color contrast on slides, and avoid using color as the only way to distinguish anything.
Keep on-screen text large enough to read on a phone.
copyright: Clear permission for any music, stock footage, or clips you didn't create.
Every image, figure, and chart in your slides needs to be yours or cleared.
If anyone other than you appears on camera, you need their release.
Attribute sources on screen or in the transcript.

items.title: Reading
items.short: Articles or guides that deepen understanding.
items.what: Learner-facing text used to explain, extend, or provide reference material. Best for anything learners will want to scan, search, or return to later.
pedagogy: Provide the complete text, not an outline.
Strong for reference material, worked examples, and step-by-step instructions.
Readings are the right home for supporting files — glossaries, templates, setup guides — because items in the learning path travel with your content if it's ever moved.
accessibility: Describe every meaningful image in alt text; mark purely decorative images as decorative.
Use real headings and lists so screen readers can navigate the structure.
Write descriptive link text rather than "click here."
Give tables real header rows, and avoid using tables purely for layout.
copyright: Confirm permission for every image, figure, table, and excerpt that isn't yours.
Attribute sources, and keep a record of what you cleared and where it came from.
Link to paywalled articles rather than reproducing them.
Course content reaches a global public audience — classroom fair-use reasoning generally doesn't carry over.

items.title: Audio Podcast
items.what: A recognized instructional format alongside video and readings. Audio suits interviews, expert conversations, and narrative explanation — anything a learner might absorb while commuting or walking.
pedagogy: Best for conversation, storytelling, and expert perspective — not for anything visual.
Considerably faster and cheaper to produce than video, which makes it a practical way to add variety.
Keep episodes focused on one idea, same as video.
Audio is a poor fit for content learners will need to reference later — reach for a reading instead.
accessibility: A full transcript is required. There's no visual channel at all, so the transcript is the only alternative.
Identify speakers by name in the transcript.
Keep audio quality clean — background noise disproportionately affects listeners using hearing aids.
copyright: Clear any music beds, stings, or archival audio.
Get a release from every guest, covering the intended use.
Attribute quoted material aloud or in the transcript.

items.title: Interactive Plugin
items.short: Embedded web apps for interactive practice.
items.what: Plugins embed single-page web applications directly inside a Coursera course item, so they support nearly any experience the web can deliver — simulations, visualizers, calculators, explorable diagrams.
pedagogy: Strong choice for concepts that are easier to manipulate than to describe.
Confirm feasibility early — plugins usually need development effort your team has to plan for.
Can be ungraded, used as graded assignment questions, or wired to external tools.
Related options: code blocks, JavaScript plugins, and external tools via LTI.
accessibility: Everything needs to be operable by keyboard alone, not just mouse or touch.
Interactive controls need screen-reader labels.
Try not to rely on color alone to convey state or feedback.
Have a plan for learners who can't use the interaction at all — an equivalent reading or activity.
Verify all of this before committing to a plugin; retrofitting accessibility is expensive.
copyright: Check the license on any third-party code or library being embedded.
Confirm you can use any dataset the plugin draws on, including for a public audience.
Credit the developer or source where appropriate.

items.title: Coach Dialogue
items.short: AI-driven conversation that applies and reflects.
items.what: Dialogue items let you create AI-driven discussions that simulate interaction with a live instructor, leading learners through structured, text-based conversations designed to hit specific learning objectives. The AI guide (Coursera Coach) asks adaptive, open-ended questions and gives personalised feedback.
pedagogy: Coursera recommends at least one Dialogue item per course, and notes that including one improves learner engagement.
Write the coach goal: what should the learner think through, decide, or produce?
Provide an opening question, 2–4 follow-up areas, and a closing reflection.
Best for reflection, case analysis, ethical decisions, and complex problem-solving.
A Dialogue in the first module is a strong way to connect the topic to a learner's own goals.
Ungraded unless you specify otherwise.
accessibility: Write prompts in plain, direct language — the conversation is the whole experience.
Don't assume a learner can see an image or diagram unless you've also described it in the prompt.
Avoid idiom and culturally specific references; the audience is global.
State roughly how long the Dialogue should take so learners can plan.
copyright: Scenarios drawn from real cases need to be anonymised or cleared.
Avoid pasting copyrighted passages into prompts as source material.
Take care with anything involving real, identifiable people.

items.title: Hands-on Practice
items.what: Where learners try the skill directly with no stakes. This can be an off-platform activity with step-by-step instructions, an ungraded Coursera Lab, or in-browser coding. Labs allow trial-and-error learning with immediate feedback and no formal assessment.
pedagogy: Provide the activity plus step-by-step learner instructions and any setup details.
Labs need notebooks or files plus environment details — confirm feasibility early.
Structure activities around clear deliverables so completion can be assessed.
No stakes. This is where learners get to fail safely.
accessibility: Check that any required tool is itself accessible before you build around it.
Write instructions as numbered steps rather than a wall of prose.
Avoid requiring precise mouse work — drag-and-drop and fine positioning exclude some learners.
Offer an equivalent path where a learner can't complete the activity as designed.
copyright: Confirm you can distribute any dataset, starter file, or template you provide.
Check licenses on required tools, especially anything commercial.
Note anything that requires a learner to create an account or pay.

items.title: Practice Quiz
items.what: Assessment for learning: optional, ungraded, and not counted toward a learner's final grade. Practice quizzes help learners self-assess, catch misconceptions early, and build the confidence to apply a skill for real.
pedagogy: Coursera recommends at least one practice quiz and one practice activity per module.
Provide every question, the correct answers, and feedback for both correct and incorrect responses.
Feedback should help learners identify the error, not just mark it wrong.
Rehearse the same thinking the graded assessment will ask for.
Use them generously; they cost a learner nothing.
accessibility: Any image in a question stem needs alt text conveying what the question depends on.
Write stems in plain language; avoid double negatives and unnecessary complexity.
Avoid questions that require distinguishing colors.
Avoid time limits on practice.
copyright: Images, passages, and data used in question stems need clearing like anything else.
Avoid reusing questions from a commercial test bank without a license.

items.title: Graded Assessment
items.what: Assessment of learning: required, counted toward the final grade, and used to evaluate whether learners achieved the stated objectives. Every module needs at least one, and every course-level objective should be validated somewhere in the graded assessments.
pedagogy: A 10-question auto-graded quiz with answer-specific feedback is the common default.
Must map to the module's stated learning objectives, not trivia from a reading.
Point learners to the specific review material for anything they missed.
Regular graded checkpoints beat one high-stakes bottleneck at the end.
Coursera also recommends at least one graded project per course: an authentic, hands-on assessment learners can put in a portfolio.
For projects, AI-graded assignments and programming assignments can evaluate a submitted artifact.
accessibility: Same requirements as practice quizzes: alt text on anything the question depends on, plain-language stems, no color-only distinctions.
If a time limit is genuinely necessary, flag it early so extended-time accommodations can be arranged.
Make sure the assessment tests the skill, not a learner's ability to use an interface.
copyright: Clear any images, passages, or datasets used in questions or project briefs.
Be clear about who owns what learners submit, especially for portfolio projects.
